Title: Advantages of Limiting Car Usage: Evidence from Around the World

The modern world, heavily reliant on motor vehicles, is witnessing a transformation in thinking about transportation. Across the globe, from German suburbs, to Colombian capital cities and beyond, the value of reducing car usage is being recognized. These initiatives not only support environmental sustainability but also contribute to the enhancement of community life, reduction of pollution, and introduction of alternative, healthy modes of transportation.

Initiatives such as the one implemented in the Vauban district in Germany illustrate the potential advantages of limiting car usage on a large scale (Rosenthal, 2009). By implementing smart planning strategies such as reducing parking facilities and promoting walking, 70% of Vaubans families have given up car ownership, leading to less pollution and a more serene community environment. This initiative has exhibited a unique treatment of suburbs, proving that life in such areas can still thrive without absolute car dependency.

While car usage reduction can be seen as an experimental situation in places like Vauban, its previse is being adopted worldwide to make suburbs more accessible and less car-dependent. The US Environmental Protection Agency promotes car-reduced communities, aiming to balance out the majority of appropriations given to highways in transportation bills (Rosenthal, 2009). If realized, such changes could significantly decrease the USs greenhouse gas emissions, which count transportation as the second largest source (Rosenthal, 2013).

A direct effect of limiting vehicle use can be witnessed in cities like Paris, where a partial driving ban lifted smog rivalling that of Beijing, one of the most polluted cities globally (Duffer, 2014). This drastic measure, repeated on different days according to the car's license plate number, illustrates the immediate results that car-reduction strategies can offer in enhancing air quality.

Bogota, the capital of Colombia, offers a yearly car-free day where citizens exclusively use alternative modes of transportation, boosting public spirit and drastically reducing pollution in the process (Selsky, 2002). This not only promotes alternative means of commuting but also revitalizes the city with an air of communal cooperation. This strategy has even sparked interest in other city authorities from around the world, who may adopt the event in their cities.

Finally, the United States also appears to be experiencing a cultural shift toward limiting car usage by seeing fewer car purchases, less driving, and a decrease in issued licenses (Rosenthal, 2013). This trend, if perpetuated, could contribute substantially to achieving environmental sustainability goals. In acknowledgment of this shift, car companies are expanding their product ranges and beginning to label themselves as mobility companies (Rosenthal, 2013).

In conclusion, the advantages of limiting car usage are evident across varied global contexts. From air pollution reduction to a decrease in greenhouse gas emissions and the revamp of community life, these initiatives present compelling reasons for further exploration and consideration for adoption by other cities and nations globally. As awareness grows, the possibility of even greater collaborative steps towards a world with less car-dependent economies seems increasingly attainable.

Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. There are several reasons for this.

First and foremost, using a cell phone while driving can be very distracting and take the driver's attention away from the road. Talking, texting, or otherwise interacting with a phone requires looking at and manipulating the device. This takes the driver's eyes and hands off the wheel as well as their mind off focusing on other vehicles and pedestrians. Numerous studies have shown that driving while using a phone can impair a driver as much as having a blood alcohol level over the legal limit. 

Second, being distracted with a phone greatly increases the risk of accidents. Drivers who use phones are more likely to drift out of their lane, rear-end other vehicles, or get into crashes of other kinds. When both hands are on the wheel and full attention is on driving, reaction times are quicker and it is easier to brake, steer away from hazards, or avoid collisions. Even brief moments of distraction from a phone could cause a crash or near miss.

Third, distracted driving endangers more than just the person using the phone. Others sharing the road, like passengers, pedestrians, bicyclists and other motorists, are also put at risk by a distracted driver. Their safety should not be compromised by someone choosing to use a cell phone. Driving is a complex task that requires full focus, and phones are simply too much of a distraction to use while in control of a rapidly moving vehicle. 

In conclusion, allowing any cell phone use while driving compromises safety and increases crash risks for all road users. Drivers should keep both hands on the wheel and their full attention on the road at all times to help avoid preventable accidents. For this reason, driving and cell phone use should remain separate activities.

Dear Senator [Senator's Last Name],

I am writing to express my support for keeping the Electoral College as the method of electing the President of the United States. While there are arguments in favor of electing the president by popular vote, I believe that the Electoral College provides important advantages that should not be dismissed.

Firstly, the Electoral College ensures certainty of outcome in the presidential election. As mentioned in "In Defense of the Electoral College" by Judge Richard A. Posner, the winning candidate's share of the Electoral College usually exceeds their share of the popular vote. This means that a dispute over the outcome of an Electoral College vote is less likely compared to a dispute over the popular vote. This minimizes the chances of a prolonged election crisis and ensures a definitive result.

Secondly, the Electoral College promotes a candidate with trans-regional appeal. This method requires a presidential candidate to have support from various regions, ensuring that the president represents the entire nation. As Judge Posner explains, candidates with only regional appeal are unlikely to be successful presidents, as residents from other regions may feel disenfranchised and believe that their interests are not being prioritized. The Electoral College encourages candidates to campaign across different states and engage with voters from diverse backgrounds.

Additionally, the Electoral College incentivizes candidates to focus their campaign efforts on swing states. These are states where the outcome of the election is uncertain and can swing either way. By doing so, candidates are compelled to pay attention to issues that matter to voters in these states. This ensures that voters in swing states receive more attention and information from the candidates, allowing them to make more informed choices.

Furthermore, the Electoral College provides a balanced representation for both large and small states. As highlighted in Judge Posner's article, the Electoral College restores some weight in the political balance that large states lose due to the disproportionate apportionment of the Senate. By granting more electoral votes to larger states, presidential candidates are encouraged to address the concerns and needs of these states. This ensures that the interests of both large and small states are taken into account during the election process.

Lastly, the Electoral College eliminates the need for run-off elections in the event that no candidate receives a majority of the votes cast. This simplifies the election process and avoids potential complications that may arise from run-off elections. By providing a clear winner, the Electoral College ensures that the will of the people is accurately represented.

While there are valid arguments against the Electoral College, such as those presented in Bradford Plumer's article "The Indefensible Electoral College," it is important to consider the practical benefits that come with this method of electing the president.

In conclusion, the Electoral College provides certainty of outcome, promotes trans-regional appeal, focuses campaign efforts on swing states, balances the representation of large and small states, and avoids the need for run-off elections. These advantages are crucial for ensuring that the president elected is representative of the entire nation. Therefore, I urge you to consider the importance of preserving the Electoral College.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

Subject: The Benefits of Keeping the Electoral College

Dear [State Senator's Name],

I am writing to express my support for the Electoral College and urge you to consider the advantages it provides in determining the President of the United States. Although there are arguments in favor of moving towards a popular vote system, I firmly believe that the Electoral College is a vital component of our constitutional process and should be retained. This letter presents multiple reasons for keeping the Electoral College, based on the information provided in the accompanying passage text from the Office of the Federal Register and Judge Richard A. Posner's defense of the Electoral College.

Firstly, the Electoral College ensures certainty of outcome. In the 2012 presidential election, Barack Obama received 61.7% of the electoral vote, even though he only had a 51.3% share of the popular vote. This system guarantees a clear winner and minimizes the likelihood of disputes over the outcome. Furthermore, with almost all states following a winner-take-all approach, even a slight plurality in a state leads to a landslide electoral-vote victory. This promotes stability and avoids the need for run-off elections, as seen in the cases of Nixon in 1968 and Clinton in 1992.

Secondly, the Electoral College promotes a sense of unity and representation for all regions of the country. A presidential candidate must have trans-regional appeal as no single region has enough electoral votes to secure victory. This ensures that candidates focus on the needs and concerns of a diverse range of states, rather than solely targeting the most populous areas. Additionally, swing states gain prominence in the electoral process, encouraging candidates to address the issues specific to those states. This fosters engagement from voters in those states and helps emphasize their importance in the election.

Moreover, the Electoral College restores balance between large and small states. Although the mal-apportionment of the Senate gives smaller states an advantage in terms of representation, the Electoral College allows larger states to have more weight in the electoral process. Due to the winner-take-all method, a victory in a large state, such as Florida, carries significantly more electoral votes than a victory in a smaller state, such as Wyoming. This prevents smaller states from being overlooked and ensures that candidates address the concerns of a wide range of voters across different states.

Lastly, the Electoral College system entices voters to engage in the political process. While critics argue that supporters of candidates who are unlikely to win their state may lose motivation to vote, the truth is that voters participate in elections to express their political preferences, not with the expectation that their vote will decide the outcome. In the 2012 election, nearly half of the eligible American population voted, further exemplifying the commitment of voters to the democratic process.

In conclusion, the Electoral College plays a crucial role in our democratic system. It provides certainty of outcome, guarantees representation for all regions, promotes engagement with swing states, balances the influence of large and small states, and avoids the need for run-off elections. While there are calls to shift towards a popular vote system, it is essential to consider the benefits and stability provided by the Electoral College. I strongly urge you to vote in favor of preserving this system for the election of the President of the United States.

Thank you for your time and attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

The Electoral College is a system in which each state is allocated a number of electors equal to its number of representatives in Congress, plus its two senators. The candidate who wins the popular vote in a state receives all of that state's electoral votes, except in Maine and Nebraska, which award electoral votes by congressional district. This means that it is possible for a candidate to win the popular vote nationwide but lose the election because they did not win the most electoral votes.

This has happened five times in American history, most recently in 2016. This was a deeply undemocratic outcome, and it has led many people to call for the abolition of the Electoral College.

This is because each state, regardless of its population, has the same number of senators. This means that the votes of people in small states are worth more than the votes of people in large states.

Second, the Electoral College system is unfair. It is possible for a candidate to win the popular vote but lose the election because they did not win the most electoral votes. This has happened five times in American history, and it is likely to happen again in the future.

I hope this letter finds you in good health and spirits. I am writing to express my support for the Electoral College and argue against changing to election by popular vote for the president of the United States. As a concerned citizen, I have thoroughly studied and analyzed the information and perspectives provided in various texts, and I believe that the Electoral College system has several benefits and should be maintained.

The Electoral College, as established by the founding fathers, serves as a compromise between election by Congress and election by popular vote. It consists of 538 electors, who vote for the President and Vice President based on the state's popular vote. Each state's allotment of electors is determined by the number of representatives in the House of Representatives, plus two for the Senators.

One of the advantages of the Electoral College is the certainty of outcome. As Judge Richard A. Posner points out, disputes over the outcome of an Electoral College vote are less likely compared to disputes over the popular vote. This is because the winner of the electoral vote usually exceeds their share of the popular vote, preventing close contests. Additionally, the winner-take-all method of awarding electoral votes ensures that a slight plurality in a state results in a substantial electoral victory, preventing ties in the nationwide electoral vote.

Another benefit of the Electoral College is that it demands trans-regional appeal from presidential candidates. No single region in the United States has enough electoral votes to elect a president. Consequently, candidates must appeal to voters from various regions, preventing the concentration of power in one area. This encourages a president-elect to represent the interests of all regions and fosters a sense of inclusivity.

The focus on swing states is another advantage of the Electoral College system. Candidates direct their campaign efforts towards states where the electoral vote outcome is uncertain. This encourages voters in swing states to pay closer attention to the campaign, making them more thoughtful and informed voters. Elections should be decided by those who have thoroughly considered the candidates' policies and qualifications, and swing states provide voters with that opportunity.

Moreover, the Electoral College provides balance to the political influence of large states. Due to the mal-apportionment of the Senate, large states have less weight in the political process. However, the Electoral College ensures that presidential candidates pay attention to these states during the campaign. Even if the popular vote is close, as exemplified by Florida in 2012, winning a large state results in a significant number of electoral votes.

Finally, the Electoral College prevents the need for run-off elections. In cases where no candidate receives a majority of the votes cast, the Electoral College consistently produces a clear winner. This avoids the complications and costs associated with organizing run-off elections and ensures a decisive result. As we have seen in the past, candidates who win a majority in the Electoral College but only a plurality of the popular vote can effectively govern and lead the nation.

While the arguments against the Electoral College have been raised, such as the potential disenfranchisement of voters in non-competitive states and the perceived undemocratic nature of the system, the practical benefits of the Electoral College outweigh these concerns. It is important to weigh the historical significance and the intent of the founding fathers in establishing this system, aiming to create a more balanced and representative democracy.

In conclusion, the Electoral College provides certainty of outcome, promotes trans-regional appeal, encourages attention to swing states, balances the political influence of large states, and avoids the need for run-off elections. These practical advantages support the retention of the Electoral College system. I urge you to consider these points when weighing the decision on whether to keep or change our current method of electing the president.

Thank you for your time and attention to this matter. I trust that you will take my arguments into account when considering the future of the Electoral College.

Sincerely,

Distance education was a popular choice for many students and parents, offering convenience and support in various ways. However, it also had its limitations, which could be disadvantageous for students studying from home. These included challenges in communication, lack of competition, and missing out on the inspirational experiences from teachers. These are crucial aspects that schools provide to students, making them valuable elements that distance learning may not be able to offer.

The first notable disadvantage of distance learning is the lack of effective communication. Communication involves the exchange of information, either verbally or non-verbally. For instance, a student may watch a video and still not understand the content. Different teachers have different teaching methods, and without the opportunity for face-to-face interaction, students may struggle to grasp the lessons. Schools, on the other hand, provide students with the chance to meet teachers and professors to discuss their issues and identify their areas of struggle. This is why communication is so vital, and something that distance learning may not fully provide.

The second benefit of in-person classes over home-based learning is the element of competition. Competition involves individuals or groups striving to outperform each other. A classic example is when a student achieves the highest test score in class, motivating others to strive for even better results. Schools foster a competitive environment, which can make learning more engaging and help students prepare for exams. This is a significant advantage that distance learning may not be able to offer.

The final aspect that students may miss out on in online classes or video conferencing is the experience and inspiration from teachers and professors. Experience refers to the knowledge or skills acquired over time, while inspiration is the ability to instill confidence and desire in others. In a classroom setting, students not only learn academic subjects but also life lessons from their teachers. Teachers can share their past experiences and motivate students who are on a similar path, helping them avoid the same mistakes. This invaluable aspect is something that students may not receive outside of a traditional classroom setting.

In conclusion, attending classes in person offers students numerous benefits that they may not gain from studying at home. These include effective communication to solve problems more easily, a competitive environment, and inspirational experiences from teachers. These are elements that online learning may not be able to provide. A classroom is not just a place for lessons, but also a miniature society that prepares students for real life. This is why attending classes in person is often more beneficial than online learning at home.

I am writing to you today to express my strong support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote.

The Electoral College is an outdated and undemocratic system that has no place in our modern society. It was originally created as a compromise between those who wanted the President to be elected by Congress and those who wanted the President to be elected by a popular vote of the people. However, the Electoral College has outlived its usefulness.

In today's society, it is simply not fair that a candidate can win the Presidency without winning the popular vote. This has happened five times in American history, most recently in 2016 when Donald Trump won the Presidency despite losing the popular vote by nearly 3 million votes.

The Electoral College also gives disproportionate power to small states. In a popular vote system, each person's vote would count equally. However, in the Electoral College system, the votes of people in small states are worth more than the votes of people in large states. The Development of Driverless Cars

While driverless cars present many benefits, their widespread adoption also carries risks that warrant careful consideration. According to the article "Driverless Cars are Coming," autonomous vehicles have the potential to significantly reduce traffic accidents caused by human error. However, fully replacing human drivers with AI systems introduces technical and ethical challenges that must be addressed before driverless cars become the norm on public roads.

One of the major selling points of driverless cars is improved safety. As the article notes, human error is the primary cause of over 90% of traffic accidents. By removing fallible human judgment from the driving task, autonomous vehicles could help prevent collisions. Driverless cars are also always alert and do not become distracted, drunk, or drowsy like people do. With AI systems handling control of speed, steering and braking, roads may become much safer.

However, the article also acknowledges that currently "no vehicle is capable of handling all possible situations that could arise on public roads." Fully autonomous driving represents a major technical challenge that will take sustained progress to overcome. Edge cases that humans handle intuitively, like responding to unusual traffic disruptions, may continue to confound AI for many years. Until driverless cars can navigate all possible scenarios as capably as people, they are unlikely to translate their theoretical safety benefits into practical risk reduction on a large scale. 

Moreover, replacing human drivers with AI prompts difficult ethical questions about how autonomous vehicles should respond in accident scenarios. The article notes engineers have yet to agree on how driverless cars should prioritize avoiding collisions with other vehicles versus pedestrians. Life-and-death determinations made by software, however well-intentioned, could undermine public trust in this new technology. Establishing ethical guidelines that anticipate complex real-world situations is an important hurdle before society embraces driverless vehicles.

While driverless cars may eventually provide benefits like improved access and reduced accidents, the technology has not yet advanced to the point of reliable, fully autonomous operation without human oversight in all road conditions. Both technical and ethical concerns remain that could endanger public safety if autonomous vehicles are adopted prematurely. With more progress on solving the challenges of unforeseen situations and clarifying ethical decision-making, driverless cars may someday transform transportation. But for the time being, human judgment still exceeds artificial intelligence in many areas of driving. A cautious approach is warranted.

Summer projects provide an excellent opportunity for students to continue their learning journey during the summer break. While some students might view them as monotonous, they are indeed advantageous as they keep the students' brains active during their long vacation. However, when teachers assign these projects, they may not always be captivating or engaging for the students. During the academic year, students often enroll in subjects they are not particularly interested in, with the aim of enhancing their college applications. Summer is a period for students to take a breather from the demanding math and English classes they undertook during the academic year, and indulge in activities they are passionate about. Hence, to keep students engrossed in their summer projects, they should have a say in the type of work they undertake. For instance, a student who has read all the Percy Jackson novels would be thrilled to delve into classic Greek myths, and would relish spending part of their summer break reading Greek mythology. However, if their English teacher assigned them a reading about the struggles of the Native Americans, the student would likely procrastinate on the project until the last week of summer break, and would not retain any information and would start the new school year with a poor grade. At Generic_School, ninth-grade students were tasked with a summer reading about the civil war, a topic many students were not interested in, resulting in a poor start to the academic year. Those who were interested in the civil war or had extensive prior knowledge of it would score full marks on the project because they were either very interested in it or did not need to conduct any research to write the essay. Conversely, there were students who were not interested in researching the Civil War, some of whom were the brightest in the class, and they received a poor grade. The problem with teacher-assigned summer projects is that they cater to the interests of a few, if any, students in a particular class, resulting in grade discrepancies based on prior knowledge and interest, rather than the ability to perform a task. Therefore, if each student could select their own topic to research over the summer break, subject to the teacher's approval, there would be fewer unjust grade discrepancies among students of equal intelligence.

Research projects play a crucial role in the later stages of a student's academic journey. Therefore, students should learn how to write a compelling paper early in their academic careers, and there's no better way to achieve this than by researching a topic they find intriguing. As mentioned earlier, many students who were not interested in the topics assigned by teachers would often neglect the project or complete it the night before school resumes, resulting in a poor start to the academic year. However, the implications of this issue are more far-reaching. Summer projects are not just about learning the material; they also aim to teach students how to research effectively and write impressive essays. To achieve this most effectively, students must be interested in the topic. If they can choose their own topic, they will select one that piques their interest and will likely perform better compared to a topic they did not choose. This will enhance their essay writing and research skills in the future, and contribute to a more engaged and intelligent student body.

In conclusion, students who are mandated to undertake summer projects should be given the liberty to choose the topic they will research over the summer. Summer break is a period for students to relax and enjoy themselves, so any work they do should be interesting. Allowing students to choose their own research topics would make each individual more invested in their work. The problem with teacher-assigned summer projects is that they lead to grade discrepancies among students of equal intelligence based on their prior knowledge of a subject. Grade discrepancies should be a reflection of a student's ability to perform the task at hand, not their prior knowledge or interest in the subject, which is what happens with teacher-assigned summer projects. Dear Senator,

I am writing to express my view that the United States should change from the current Electoral College system to instead elect the president by a national popular vote. While the Electoral College system has its defenders, I believe a popular vote would be fairer and more democratic.

Some argue that the Electoral College system encourages candidates to build broader coalitions and appeal to a wide range of states. However, in recent elections we have seen candidates focus their efforts only in key swing states that could tip the electoral vote, largely ignoring the vast majority of states. This discourages voter turnout, as millions feel their votes do not truly matter in non-competitive states. A popular vote would make every American citizen's vote equally important, wherever they live, and encourage higher participation across the country. 

Critics of the popular vote point out that candidates might then focus only on densely populated urban areas. However, in today's society Americans are less regionally isolated, and campaign messages can reach rural areas cost-effectively through television and internet. A national campaign aimed at winning the popular vote would still require appealing to a diverse range of demographic and geographic groups. 

It is also argued that the Electoral College guards against instability by usually producing a clear winner. However, it nearly failed to do so in the very close 2000 election, and narrow nationwide margins could still lead to doubts about legitimacy. A popular vote would replace disputed state-by-state outcomes with a clear national result. While a candidate could still win without a majority, the minimum plurality needed would likely be larger than the electoral vote can provide.

In summary, while the Electoral College system aims to achieve representative and stable government, in practice it discourages voter participation and national consensus-building. Changing to a popular vote would make every citizen's voice equal and compel candidates to appeal to Americans across geographic and demographic divides. For these reasons, I ask that you support electoral reform and consider citizens' preference for a national popular vote.

Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones in Any Capacity While Operating a Vehicle

The use of cell phones while driving has become an epidemic issue on today's roadways. With nearly everyone owning a smartphone that can perform countless distracting functions, it has become incredibly tempting for drivers to engage with their devices while driving. However, the dangers of doing so far outweigh any perceived benefits. Using a cell phone while driving, even hands-free, can seriously endanger the lives of the driver as well as others on the road. For this reason, drivers should not be permitted to use cell phones in any capacity when operating a motor vehicle.

Numerous studies have demonstrated that driving while using a cell phone, whether it is for talking, texting, or other apps, impairs a driver's abilities in many of the same ways that drunk driving does. When focused on a phone, a driver's reaction time slows, their eyes are taken off the road for prolonged periods, and their focus shifts from the dangerous task of driving to the distractions of the phone. This puts not only the phone-using driver at risk, but also jeopardizes the safety of passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and other motorists sharing the road. Even hands-free use of a cell phone for calls is distracting as the mental capacity required for holding a phone conversation diverts the brain from full attention to the complex act of navigating a vehicle. 

Beyond impaired abilities, cell phone use has been directly linked to an alarming increase in car accidents in recent years. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that roadway collisions due to cell phone distraction result in over 1 million crashes annually. Being on a phone while driving makes accidents and near-misses far more likely to occur. Texting especially has proven to be an extremely hazardous behavior, as it requires drivers to take their eyes completely off the road for prolonged periods of time. But even hands-free phone conversations or general device manipulation introduces unnecessary cognitive strain into the critical task of driving.

With how widespread and accepted cell phone use has become in daily life, a total ban may seem like an unrealistic goal. However, for the safety of all road users, drivers must be responsible for avoiding phone distraction. Alternatives like Bluetooth, pull over areas, or do not disturb modes can help discourage impulsive phone behaviors that endanger lives. Most importantly, motorists need to recognize that driving is a complex task that deserves full mental engagement, not competition with cell phone activities, if we want safer roadways. For the protection of both drivers and the public, a complete prohibition of cell phone use while operating a vehicle is ultimately the most prudent solution.

Summer break from schools has been a topic of consideration for a long time. Many people do not appreciate a summer break because they forget school material too easily throughout those few months of no school. Others say the break is beneficial due to the fact that students' minds are given a while to rest. Some schools have been combating the loss of knowledge over the summer by giving mandatory projects for students to complete over the summer. By doing this, they are assuring that the students do not forget too much and are still able to function well at the beginning of the next school year. The issue comes in on the differing ideas that these summer projects should be teacher-designed or student-designed. In the schools that require summer projects, the projects should be student-designed.

Schools have given summer breaks with the means of giving both teachers and students a rest. But due to such a large gap in between classes, students have often been observed to forget many things and therefore need lots of review at the beginning of school, which takes up lots of needed class time. If we spend lots of time reviewing at the beginning of each school year, the date for the end of school gets pushed farther into summer, therefore decreasing the amount of break. If students are given projects to design and complete over the summer, they will remember much more. Allowing students to design a project themselves gets them more involved with the material, thus causing them to learn more efficiently than in the classroom. When they are independent and outside of school, the willingness to complete a project would improve quite a bit, even if it is over their break. The end result of this would be that there would be less time taken up to review at the beginning of school, and new material would be presented much sooner, leading to an earlier end date for school, and, obviously, and longer summer break.

With a mandatory summer project that is teacher-designed, the teacher gets even less of a break. Instead of looking forward to the end of school and a nice, long break from the patience-draining teenagers, they have to worry about creating projects for all their students. Since they are already so tremendously busy, heaping yet another material requirement on their head would be unfair. They already do so much more work than the students, so why not make the students create their own projects? Many of my teachers have talked about how over breaks (like winter and spring break) they did lots of grading and planning for when school starts back up. Seeing as how winter and spring breaks would be the only good times to work on a summer project, they would have to be designing a project on top of grading and planning. Consequently, the teachers become more stressed and burdened, all the while not receiving an increase in their salary. Student-designed projects would allow teachers to not be as stressed, and allow them to have more of a break than they otherwise would.

Personally, I would enjoy having to design my own project for summer break. It would give me something more to do, and if it's designed by me, I would find it vastly more enjoyable than one created by the teacher. In my experience, I have quickly forgotten lots of school material in the span of summer break. Summer break is already a time in my life where I hardly do anything except a couple vacations and lounging around at home. If I had to design my project, my brain would be up and running and I would be finding much more to do. Instead of being sedentary, I could be furthering my knowledge in certain subjects so that I feel more prepared for the following school year. My imagination could also run more free than it normally does. Having to create something ourselves allows our minds to be more free and imaginative. Deep down, imagination is something we all crave, but it is suppressed quite often by requirements and rubrics. Minds young and old long to be free and not confined to what we are told we have to do or should do. Making us students design our own summer projects gives our minds wings and something to do.

A summer project is a good idea, but whether or not it should be designed by the student or by the teacher is still under thought. The benefits of having student-designed projects far outweigh those of having teacher-designed projects. Letting students make their own project allows them to increase their consumption of knowledge of different subjects because they are not sitting in a classroom and being talked to by a teacher. They can do what they want with that subject, making it more enjoyable for them and allowing them to remember more, thus decreasing the need to review for a couple of weeks at the beginning of every school year. Another benefit is that teachers would not have to be worked even more. They are already worked hard for so little pay, so they should not have to worry about creating even more material for students. A student-designed project allows the freedom of imagination. Schools preach the idea that they want students to be free of mind, yet they still have a multitude of confines. Many of us also do not do much during summer break, and if we are able to create something that we would enjoy completing, we would be quite a bit more occupied during the summer. We would be excited to go back to school and share what we learned or did over the summer. For these reasons, student-designed summer projects would be a much more beneficial and accepted form of education over the break.

Upon first observation of images captured by the Viking orbiter in 1976, the Face on Mars appeared to be a carved structure on the surface of the red planet. However, further analysis by NASA scientists has revealed that what was seen is simply a natural landform created through geological processes over billions of years. 

One of the key pieces of evidence supporting the natural origin of the Face is its scale. Measuring only around 1 km in length, the Feature is far too small to clearly depict a human face from such a distance in space. For an alien civilization to construct a structure recognizable from orbit, it would need to be enormous, several kilometers across at minimum. Additionally, while some straight lines can be seen, there is no evidence of sculpting or artifice upon closer examination. The shapes are inconsistent with being man-made.

Another important factor is geology. Mars, like Earth, has experienced extensive erosion from wind and dust storms over eons. Numerical modeling of these weathering effects has demonstrated how less resistant rock layers underlying harder rocks in the area could naturally result in features resembling eyes, nose, and mouth through varied erosion rates across different strata. Exposed rock layers in the region also contain the same mixtures as those that make up the Face feature, indicating it formed from the same underlying natural materials. 

In conclusion, while an alien-carved structure would be fascinating, there is simply no compelling evidence the Face on Mars is anything other than a coincidental arrangement of natural geological patterns that only take on a human likeness from our perspective. As scientists, we must follow the evidence, not bizarre claims lacking supportive facts. All available data conclusively demonstrates the Face is a natural landform, not an artificial construction. Though not as exciting as the possibility of alien contact, the real geological history of Mars revealed through scientific study is marvel enough.

One of the primary arguments against the Electoral College is that it appears undemocratic, as the president is ultimately elected by electors rather than the popular vote (Posner 15). Another key argument in favor of the Electoral College is that it encourages voters in swing states to engage closely with the election process (Posner 20). ### Limiting Car Usage: A Smart Choice for Individuals and Society

Cars have become an essential part of our lives. We use them to get to work, school, and the grocery store. We take them on vacation and to visit friends and family. But our reliance on cars has come at a cost. Cars contribute to air pollution, climate change, and traffic congestion. They also make us less active and more isolated.

There are many reasons to limit car usage. For one, cars contribute to air pollution. When we drive, our cars release pollutants into the air that can cause respiratory problems, heart disease, and cancer. Air pollution is a major public health concern, and it is especially harmful to children, the elderly, and people with asthma or other respiratory problems.

Cars also contribute to climate change. When we drive, our cars release greenhouse gases into the atmosphere that trap heat and cause the planet to warm. Climate change is already having a significant impact on our planet, and it is only going to get worse if we do not take action to reduce our emissions.

In addition to air pollution and climate change, cars also contribute to traffic congestion. When we drive, we add to the number of cars on the road, which can make it difficult to get around. Traffic congestion can waste time and fuel, and it can also be a source of stress and frustration.

Cars also make us less active. When we drive, we do not get the same amount of exercise as we would if we walked, biked, or took public transportation. This can lead to obesity and other health problems.

Finally, cars can make us more isolated. When we drive, we are less likely to interact with our neighbors and the people around us. This can lead to a sense of loneliness and isolation.

While the Facial Action Coding System that can identify human emotions may seem beneficial in reading students' engagement in the classroom, its use risks violating student privacy and fundamental rights.

In conclusion, while the intent of using this technology is to help improve education, its application to constantly monitor students risks violating student consent and privacy. For student well-being and development, alternative approaches that do not compromise their autonomy or subject them to continuous surveillance should be explored instead. Driverless cars have the potential to revolutionize transportation, but there are also significant risks associated with their development. In this essay, I will argue that the benefits of driverless cars outweigh the risks.

**Benefits of Driverless Cars**

There are a number of benefits to be gained from the development of driverless cars. First, driverless cars would make roads safer. Human error is a major cause of traffic accidents, and driverless cars would eliminate this risk. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), 94% of traffic accidents are caused by human error. Driverless cars would also be able to communicate with each other, reducing the risk of collisions.

Second, driverless cars would reduce congestion. Traffic congestion is a major problem in many cities, and driverless cars could help to alleviate this problem. Driverless cars would be able to drive more efficiently, and they could also be used to provide shared transportation services, which would reduce the number of cars on the road.

The government or corporations could use driverless cars to track people's movements.

**Conclusion**

The benefits of driverless cars outweigh the risks. Driverless cars would make roads safer, reduce congestion, and make travel more convenient. The risks of driverless cars can be mitigated through proper regulation. In conclusion, I believe that the development of driverless cars is a positive step for society.

Seeking multiple opinions when making an important decision or choice is beneficial for several reasons. Getting different perspectives allows one to consider options they may have otherwise overlooked. It also prevents becoming too narrow in one's thinking. When we talk to just one person, we risk only hearing views similar to our own biases. However, talking to more than one person exposes us to new information and ways of thinking about the issue. This can help us make a choice that considers more angles.

For example, if someone was deciding between two job offers, seeking advice from just one friend may mean only hearing about factors like salary, location or hours that most appeal to that friend. However, getting input from multiple people, like other friends, family members or former coworkers, would provide a more well-rounded picture. One person may focus on career growth opportunities, another on company culture, while a third suggests considering personal fulfillment over other priorities. Balancing these varied views helps one identify under which offer they would be happiest and most successful in the long run. 

Another key benefit is that multiple opinions help to minimize error. Any one person may give a biased or partially inaccurate perspective due to their own limited experience. But getting more inputs decreases the likelihood of being mislead, as individual biases cancel each other out. One advisor could overlook an important downside, but another may catch that critical factor. Looking at all options holistically after hearing from several trusted sources leads to a decision grounded in reality, not tunnel vision.

In summary, seeking multiple opinions provides the advantage of exposure to new ideas, a broader range of considerations, and error-checking to make the strongest possible choice. While any one person's advice could hypothetically suffice, discussing major decisions with a variety of sources helps avoid overlooking key details to make the choice most likely to lead to satisfaction in the long run. A multifaceted view leads to wiser decision making.

The candidate who wins the popular vote in a state receives all of that state's electoral votes, except in Maine and Nebraska, which award their electoral votes proportionally.

This means that millions of Americans' votes were essentially thrown away.

Second, the Electoral College gives disproportionate power to small states. This is because each state, regardless of its population, gets at least three electoral votes. This means that a voter in Wyoming has more than twice the voting power of a voter in California.

Third, the Electoral College encourages candidates to focus their campaigns on a handful of "swing states," where the race is close. This means that voters in many states are essentially ignored by the candidates.

I believe that the United States should elect its President by popular vote. This would be the fairest and most democratic way to choose our leader. It would also ensure that every vote counts. I urge you to support a constitutional amendment that would abolish the Electoral College and elect the President by popular vote.

Lastly, some argue that extended hours could extend to a loss of valuable sleep, resulting in poorer learning outcomes.

In conclusion, there are some valid arguments both for and against extending school hours. However, when weighing the pros and cons, it is important to take all factors into consideration and ensure that any potential policy changes are in the best interests of all involved.

While distance learning offers flexibility and convenience, I do not think it provides the same benefits as in-person learning. There are several reasons why attending classes from home may not be as effective for students.

First, learning from home could hinder social development. At school, students have daily interactions with teachers and classmates that help them learn key social skills. They practice teamwork, compromise, and communication through group projects. Students also form meaningful friendships that support their social and emotional growth. Much of this peer interaction is lost with distance learning. 

Second, it can be difficult for students to stay focused and motivated at home. There are many distractions at home like phones, TV, chores and siblings. It requires a high level of self-discipline for students to avoid these distractions and pay attention during online lessons. Younger students especially may struggle without the structure of a classroom. 

Third, hands-on learning is limited with distance education. Some subjects like science, art and physical education benefit greatly from hands-on demonstrations and experiments that simply can't be replicated virtually. Distance learning also makes it harder for teachers to assess student understanding and provide guidance through one-on-one support. Any technical issues like unstable internet connection can further disrupt the learning process.

While distance learning has its advantages in offering flexibility, especially in unique situations, I believe the traditional classroom setting provides a better overall education. For students' social-emotional development and to support different learning styles, the structured environment and peer interactions of in-person school are difficult to replace. Attending classes at school seems to be the better choice for benefiting students.

At that time, it made sense to have a system that gave more power to small states. However, the United States has since grown and changed dramatically, and the Electoral College is no longer an effective way to elect the President.

The Electoral College is unfair because it gives more power to some states than others. In a presidential election, each state is awarded a number of electoral votes equal to its number of Senators and Representatives in Congress. This means that the votes of people in small states are worth more than the votes of people in large states. For example, a voter in Wyoming has 3.65 times more voting power than a voter in California.

The Electoral College also leads to a situation where the candidate who wins the popular vote does not always become President. This has happened five times in American history, most recently in 2000. In 2000, George W. Bush won the Electoral College but lost the popular vote to Al Gore. This led to a great deal of controversy and distrust in the election process.

I believe that the best way to ensure that our elections are fair and representative of the will of the people is to elect the President by popular vote. This would give every voter equal power and would ensure that the candidate who wins the most votes becomes President.

I urge you to support a constitutional amendment that would abolish the Electoral College and elect the President by popular vote. This is the best way to ensure that our elections are fair and representative of the will of the people.

Sincerely,

Dear Principal Smith, 

I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed policy change that would require students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports and other extracurricular activities. While maintaining good grades is important, I do not think tying eligibility to such a high standard is fair or will have the intended effects. 

Requiring a B average will negatively impact many students who currently have a C average. Extracurricular activities are important for developing skills, staying active, managing stress, and finding belonging in the school community. For some students, participating in a sport or club is what keeps them motivated and engaged in their overall education. Taking this away could damage their self-esteem and reduce their commitment to academic improvement. A C average already shows that students are passing their classes, and participating in after-school activities may help them elevate their performance over time. 

Imposing a B average could create unrealistic pressure that backfires. Students may feel so stressed about keeping their grades up that their performance declines. They may lose focus on learning for learning's sake and instead prioritize grades over comprehension. Some students simply struggle more in certain subjects no matter how hard they try, through no fault of their own. Punishing these students seems unfair. 

A better approach would be to create incentive programs rather than use strict eligibility rules. For example, any student who raises their grade from a C to a B within a quarter could have activities fees reduced or waived. Tutoring and mentoring programs could also help those committed to improving. This rewards effort and progress over an arbitrary average.

In closing, while maintaining academic standards is understandable, tying extracurricular eligibility to a B average will harm more students than it helps. I urge you to reconsider this policy and instead try incentive programs that motivate without punishing. The developmental well-being of students should be the top priority.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

The use of Facial Action Coding System (FACS) technology to read student emotions in the classroom could provide both benefits and drawbacks. On one hand, this technology may help teachers gain insights into how their lessons are landing with students and whether they are engaging or boring certain individuals. If a teacher notices multiple students appear bored or confused during part of a lesson, FACS could alert them to adjust their approach or add more examples to improve understanding. It could also help teachers identify students who are struggling silently and may need additional assistance. 

However, there are also valid privacy and implementation concerns. Continuous monitoring of student facial expressions may make some feel uncomfortable or insecure, like they are being scrutinized. Young teenagers especially may feel self-conscious about teachers analyzing their every emotional reaction. There is also a risk that teachers could misinterpret what emotions mean in context or draw incorrect conclusions about how students are processing new information. Subtle facial ticks may not always correlate directly with emotional states. Relying too much on technology instead of also talking with students could damage relationships and trust in the classroom.

Overall, while FACS technology in theory could provide useful feedback to teachers, the practical challenges may outweigh the benefits, especially for younger students. More pilot testing would need to be done to show it can be implemented without compromising student well-being or privacy. Rather than constant monitoring, an occasional survey of student engagement through FACS may strike a better balance. Most important is that technology supports, but does not replace, human classroom interactions between teachers and their students.

However, in recent elections we have seen candidates focus their efforts only on key swing states while largely ignoring the vast majority of states. This can make some states feel ignored and disenfranchised. With a popular vote, candidates would theoretically need to appeal to a broader range of demographics across the whole country rather than catering only to swing state interests. 

It is also argued that without the Electoral College, candidates might only campaign in urban areas with larger populations. However, in today's era candidates already rely heavily on mass media and can reach voters anywhere. Rural voters would still be able to make their voices heard. Additionally, our system should strive to give each vote equal weight regardless of what state someone lives in. With the popular vote, every vote nationwide would directly influence the outcome rather than some votes effectively being worth more than others based on what state they happen to be cast in.

Some point out structural benefits the Electoral College provides, but it can also result in presidents being elected despite losing the nationwide popular vote. This has occurred a few times in history already and erodes many citizens' faith in the democratic process. A popular vote system would select presidents based purely on which candidate the actual majority of American people support. While removing the Electoral College may not be a perfect solution, I believe it would create a more representative system that leaves less chance for doubts about fairness and legitimacy. For these reasons, I encourage you to support a popular vote for electing the president in the future.

Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. There are several compelling reasons for this. 

First and foremost, using a cell phone while driving is dangerous and distracting. When a person is driving, their full attention should be on the road and other vehicles. However, cell phones provide many distractions - whether it's talking, texting, or using apps. These distractions take a driver's attention away from where it needs to be. Numerous studies have shown that using a cell phone while driving can reduce situational awareness and increase the risk of accidents as much as having a blood alcohol concentration over the legal driving limit. 

Secondly, cell phone use provides manual distractions as well. Even hands-free options require some level of manual interaction that takes a driver's hands off the wheel. Answering or ending a call, changing the music, or adjusting the volume all require brief manipulation that diverts attention. Manual distractions also delay a driver's ability to react in an emergency scenario. With response times being so critical on the road, any delay can put lives in jeopardy. 

Finally, cell phone bans help set a clear standard for safe driving behavior. Allowing some cell phone use but not other uses would be difficult to regulate and enforce. An outright ban sends a unambiguous message that driving requires full attention. It also encourages drivers to get into the habit of turning phones off or putting them away before getting behind the wheel. 

In summary, the dangers of distraction from cell phone use outweigh any perceived benefits. A total ban of cell phones while driving is justified to help curb accidents and save lives on our roads. Public safety must be the top priority, and unfettered cell phone use compromises that safety. For these compelling reasons, drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity when operating a motor vehicle.

Is it more beneficial for summer projects to be designed by students or teachers? Many schools mandate a summer project for students to ensure they have some form of academic engagement during the break. It is generally more advantageous for the teacher to devise the summer project. Teachers are equipped with the skills to assign work that is appropriate for their students. Therefore, projects should be designed by teachers as they understand the nature of work to assign their students, they typically wouldn't assign something excessively unusual, and they wouldn't make it as simplistic as the students might.

Some might contend that students will push themselves and not make it too easy. Others might argue that some teachers assign tasks that are somewhat eccentric and could be overly challenging. Some might also suggest that students have numerous commitments over the summer, such as jobs and sports, or even both. However, not all students have these obligations, and those who do should allocate a little time for their projects. Furthermore, teachers should design projects because they understand what kind of project to create for the students.

The primary reason why summer projects should be teacher-designed is that teachers understand what type of project to assign. This is because teachers, having likely assigned projects for years, understand what type of projects might be too difficult or too easy for some students. By the time summer arrives, most teachers will have a good understanding of their students' capabilities and limitations, and they know whether to make the project challenging or somewhat easy. Teachers strive to avoid making the projects too difficult for students to complete. For instance, a teacher wouldn't instruct their students to read, say, ten books and then summarize them, because they understand that not every student has the time to complete it if they have other commitments. Secondly, teachers wouldn't assign something that seemed excessively unusual or strange.

Teachers wouldn't assign a project that was eccentric and strange. For instance, a teacher wouldn't instruct you to write five full essays in MLA style, both handwritten and typed. The reason is that even though summer may seem lengthy, it can actually pass by very quickly, and many students have commitments during that time. For example, a student may have a sport that requires daily practice or a job that requires them to work every day. Bearing this in mind, teachers would make it challenging but would try to avoid making the projects excessively unusual. Another reason why teachers wouldn't assign a strange project could also be that not all teachers want to grade a lot of papers. For instance, if they were to assign something like a few essays and a reading project, the grading they would have to do is much more than the work the students had to do, simply because there are a lot of students who may have completed the work. In addition to teachers not making the projects eccentric and strange, they would also not make the project as easy as the students might.

Finally, summer projects should be teacher-designed because teachers wouldn't make the projects as easy as the students might. Students usually prefer not to do anything over summer because they view it as their break from work and projects, so if the school allowed the students to design them, the students might make it very easy to avoid doing much. Students would exploit the opportunity to design their own projects. For instance, students might create an easy project like reading a comic book or something similar and not do much. The teacher, however, will make it somewhat challenging. For example, they will assign a project that wouldn't be very easy but will make it somewhat difficult. Not all students will make it easy; there are some students who will challenge themselves to do well and create a good project. But it would be more effective if the teacher were to design it. In conclusion, it would be more efficient if the teacher were to design the summer project.

In conclusion, teachers should design the summer reading project because they understand what to assign to their students, they won't make it eccentric or strange, and they also won't make it as easy as the students might. Teachers are paid to teach students, so it would make sense if the teachers were to assign the summer projects because they know what type of assignments to give to the students. After all of this is considered, it becomes clear why teachers should design the summer projects and why students should not be allowed to.

Its design promotes a sense of inclusivity by requiring candidates to appeal nationwide instead of focusing on specific regions, even though they might heavily favor one candidate over another (Posner, 19).

However, I acknowledge the concerns raised by Bradford Plumer in "The Indefensible Electoral College," especially about the system's lack of direct democracy and the potential for 'faithless' electors (Plumer, 9, 11). Yet it's important to note that the founding fathers established the Electoral College precisely as a compromise between election by Congress and election by popular vote (Office of the Federal Register, 1). This compromise continues to serve as an acknowledgement that the United States is a federation of states, not a monolithic entity. 

The argument Plumer presents related to the potential disparity between the popular vote and the election outcome has indeed materialized on a few occasions, but it's important to remember that such instances are rare (Posner, 16). Implementing a direct election system may shine a light on populous states, but it could also alienate less populated ones due to the candidates focus on cities and locations with a high concentration of voters (Posner, 21). In such a scenario, several regions of the country might feel underrepresented or overlooked, creating a divide that could be more damaging to the nation's unity.

As the understanding of the electoral process differs among citizens, perhaps a more productive solution than outright abolishment of the Electoral College would be education about this mechanism's significance and operation. This could help minimize the confusion and concerns raised regarding the electoral process whilst preserving the benefits of the current system.

In conclusion, although the Electoral College may not be a perfect system, it has stood the test of time by delivering stable, generally accepted outcomes while maintaining a relative balance of power among states. Therefore, our focus, rather than discarding it, should be to enhance understanding of its workings and purpose.

As a 9th grade student, I have been learning about the Electoral College and its role in the presidential election process. I understand that there are differing opinions on whether to keep the Electoral College or switch to a popular vote system. After researching and analyzing the information, I believe that the Electoral College should be kept in place.

One of the main arguments in favor of the Electoral College is that it ensures certainty of outcome. With the Electoral College, the candidate who wins the most votes in a state gets all of that state's electoral votes, which almost always leads to a clear winner. This is important because it allows for a peaceful transfer of power and avoids the possibility of a drawn-out election process. In addition, the Electoral College requires candidates to have broad, transregional appeal. This means that presidential candidates must consider the needs and opinions of voters across the country, rather than just focusing on one region or group of people.

Another argument in favor of the Electoral College is that it focuses attention on swing states. Swing states are states that are not consistently red or blue, and are therefore crucial in determining the outcome of the election. This focus on swing states leads to more representation for voters in those states, as presidential candidates must listen to their concerns and address their issues. Additionally, the Electoral College balances the influence of large states. Without the Electoral College, large states like California and Texas would have a disproportionate amount of influence over the election, while smaller states would be ignored. The Electoral College ensures that all states have an equal say in the election.

Furthermore, the Electoral College avoids the need for run-off elections. In a popular vote system, it is possible for a candidate to win with a small plurality of votes, rather than a majority. This would lead to a run-off election, which would be costly and time-consuming. The Electoral College eliminates the need for run-off elections, as the candidate with the most electoral votes is automatically declared the winner.

I understand that some argue that the Electoral College is undemocratic and leads to voter disenfranchisement in states dominated by a single party. However, I believe that these concerns are outweighed by the benefits of the Electoral College. The Electoral College ensures that the president is elected in a way that is representative of the country as a whole, rather than just the most populated areas. It also ensures that the president is accountable to voters across the country, rather than just a select few.

In conclusion, I believe that the Electoral College should be kept in place. It ensures certainty of outcome, requires candidates to have broad appeal, focuses attention on swing states, balances the influence of large states, and avoids the need for run-off elections. While some may argue that the Electoral College is undemocratic, I believe that its benefits outweigh its drawbacks. I urge you to consider the importance of the Electoral College in ensuring a fair and representative presidential election process.

Schools require summer projects to help students continue learning even during their break from regular classes. However, there is debate around whether these projects should be teacher-designed or student-designed. I believe summer projects are best designed by the students themselves for a few key reasons. 

When students have autonomy in designing their own summer work, it promotes intrinsic motivation to learn. If students get to choose a topic they find genuinely interesting or meaningful, they are more likely to fully engage with the work and get something valuable from it. On the other hand, if a project is chosen by the teacher without input from the student, there is a greater risk of it feeling like a chore rather than an opportunity. This can undermine the educational purpose of having a summer assignment at all.

Allowing student-designed projects also empowers students and gives them a sense of ownership over their own education. By treating students as active participants in deciding how they spend their break time learning, it respects them as individuals and encourages self-guided inquiry. This type of approach fosters independence, creativity and lifelong learning skills that will serve students well beyond their school years. 

Of course, teacher guidance would still have an important role even with student-designed projects. Teachers could provide parameters around appropriate topics or types of work. They could also be available for consultation as students develop their project ideas. But the core task--what specific question to explore or issue to address--should stem from the natural interests of each student. 

In conclusion, giving students ownership over designing their own summer learning projects through choices that excite their individual interests and curiosity is key to keeping education meaningful and engaging during the break from school. This approach promotes intrinsic motivation, empowerment, and skills for independent learning--far better outcomes than relegating summer work to just another task assigned by teachers. For these reasons, I believe summer projects are best led by the students themselves.

I am writing to express my support for the continuation of the Electoral College in the election of the President of the United States. While there are arguments on both sides of this issue, I believe that the Electoral College system has served our nation well for over two centuries and should be maintained.

One of the main advantages of the Electoral College is its ability to provide certainty of outcome. As stated by Judge Richard Posner in his article, a dispute over the outcome of an Electoral College vote is less likely than a dispute over the popular vote. This is because the winning candidate's share of the Electoral College usually exceeds their share of the popular vote. Furthermore, the winner-take-all system ensures that even a slight plurality in a state can result in a landslide electoral-vote victory. While it is not impossible for a tie in the nationwide electoral vote to occur, it is highly unlikely. This certainty helps provide stability and legitimacy to the election process.

Another argument in favor of the Electoral College is that it ensures every region of the country is taken into account during the election. With the need to appeal to a wide range of states, candidates are encouraged to campaign in different regions and address the concerns and interests of voters across the nation. This helps prevent a candidate with only regional appeal from becoming president and ensures that the interests of all regions are considered. As Judge Posner points out, this is crucial for maintaining a united and representative federal government.

The Electoral College also encourages candidates to focus their campaign efforts on swing states. These states, where the outcome is less predictable, receive the most attention and the most thoughtful voters. This ensures that the decision of the election is made by those who have closely evaluated the candidates and their policies. By focusing on swing states, candidates are encouraged to address the needs and concerns of a diverse range of voters, resulting in a more balanced and representative election process.

Additionally, the Electoral College provides a balance of power between large and small states. As Judge Posner notes, large states receive more attention from presidential candidates due to the additional electoral votes they have. This helps to counterbalance the mal-apportionment of the Senate, where small states have an equal number of senators despite having smaller populations. This ensures that the interests of both large and small states are taken into account during the election process.

Lastly, the Electoral College prevents the need for run-off elections when no candidate receives a majority of the votes cast. This avoids the complications and costs associated with organizing and conducting additional elections. Instead, the Electoral College invariably produces a clear winner, ensuring a smooth transition of power and stability in our democracy.

While there are arguments against the Electoral College, such as the belief that it is unfair to voters and encourages candidates to focus on swing states only, I believe that the advantages of this system outweigh these concerns. The Electoral College provides certainty, encourages a trans-regional appeal, focuses campaign efforts on swing states, balances power between large and small states, and avoids run-off elections.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that the Electoral College should be maintained as the method of selecting the President of the United States. Its ability to provide certainty, consider the interests of different regions, encourage candidates to campaign widely, balance power between large and small states, and prevent run-off elections make it a valuable and necessary part of our democratic process. I urge you to consider these arguments and support the continuation of the Electoral College.

At first thought, distance learning may seem like an easy way out for kids who just want to skip school to not be held accountable for it; however, while it may seem counter-intuitive to allow students to decide to take their classes online, it can often times be very beneficial for both those who take advantage of the option and those who continue a traditional path of school. By allowing students the option to choose their learning environment then it lets students decide whether they learn best from the comfort of their own home, a classroom, or anywhere else. In addition, giving students the option to decide where and how they learn best allows more sick students to stay home rather than come to school because they won't have to worry about falling behind on schoolwork. Some people may think distance learning is just a way for kids to take an easy way out of their education, simply because they are lazy; when, in fact, distance learning is not only a way for children to experience different class styles, but it is also a way for students to do their part in reducing the spread of communicable diseases.

It is a common belief that the best education comes from inside a classroom and other means of education are somehow lesser than a classroom education. This may be true for many people but it is definitely not true for everyone. Classrooms are often loud and crowded which allows even the most well intentioned students the chance to be distracted by their peers. Sometimes these classrooms are almost uncontrollable which leads the teachers to stop even trying to teach. This, in turn, leaves students who truly wanted to learn at a disadvantage because now their teacher has lost their motivation to teach. Distance learning can not only reduce the physical class sizes and make them more manageable, but it can also allow students who have a tendency to be more rowdy the option to see if removing themselves from the presence of people helps them focus better on their work. While they may be able to make it through all of their classes without much issue, the burden now falls onto all their classmates who were in contact with them all day. By allowing students to do distance learning, this issue of attendance is eliminated because the students who are sick but not suffering too heavily from the symptoms will be allowed to attend their classes from home so they can take the day off to help prevent the spread of illness without having to worry about all the work they may have missed. In addition, this can help a variety of students who miss school for extended periods of time because of issues such as injury, hospitalization, and even some mental health issues.
